cards.title: Asteroids, the rocks between planets
cards.summary: An asteroid is a rocky or metal-rich object that moves around the Sun. Many asteroids are found between Mars and Jupiter, in a wide area called the asteroid belt.

cards.title: Atoms, the tiny pieces of matter
cards.summary: Air, water, rocks, and your own body are made of pieces called atoms. They are far too small to see with your eyes.

cards.title: Australia
cards.summary: Australia is a country in the Southern Hemisphere. Much of the middle is dry.

cards.title: Bats and how they find their way
cards.summary: Bats are mammals and can fly by flapping their wings. Their wings are made of thin skin stretched over long fingers.

cards.title: Brazil
cards.summary: Brazil is the largest country in South America by area. Its eastern edge is along the Atlantic Ocean.

cards.title: Canada
cards.summary: Canada covers a large part of North America, from the Atlantic Ocean in the east to the Pacific Ocean in the west and the Arctic Ocean to the north. A trip across it can take you through rocky mountains, broad plains, forests, and lakes.

cards.title: Density and why some things float
cards.summary: If you have two blocks the same size, one may feel much heavier. More matter is packed into that block’s space, so it is denser.

cards.title: Earth, our home planet
cards.summary: Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only place where we know life exists. Most of its surface is covered by water.

cards.title: Earth’s moving plates
cards.summary: Earth’s stiff outer shell is broken into huge pieces called tectonic plates. They fit together a little like puzzle pieces, but they move very slowly.

cards.title: Egypt
cards.summary: Egypt is a country mostly in northeastern Africa. Much of its land is desert, while fields and cities lie along the Nile River.

cards.title: France
cards.summary: Most of France’s land is in western Europe. Paris, its capital, grew along the Seine River.

cards.title: Galaxies and the Milky Way
cards.summary: A galaxy is an enormous group of stars, gas, and dust held together by gravity. Some galaxies have swirling arms, others look like smooth blobs, and some have no neat shape.

cards.title: Gravity, the pull between objects
cards.summary: Gravity is a pull between objects that have mass. A ball falls to the floor because Earth pulls it down.

cards.title: How a solar eclipse works
cards.summary: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon crosses in front of the Sun as seen from part of Earth. The Moon’s shadow falls on a patch of Earth.

cards.title: How an electric circuit makes a light work
cards.summary: An electric circuit gives electric charges a path to move along. In a simple flashlight, the battery, bulb, and wires can make a loop.

cards.title: How atoms join to make molecules
cards.summary: A molecule is a group of atoms joined together. One water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

cards.title: How can 1/2 and 2/4 be equal?
cards.summary: Draw two strips of the same length. Divide one into two equal parts and shade one part.

cards.title: How can you count syllables in a word?
cards.summary: A syllable is one sound part of a spoken word. Say rainbow slowly and listen for two parts, rain and bow.

cards.title: How clouds form
cards.summary: A cloud is a group of very small water drops, ice crystals, or both. Air can carry water as an invisible gas called water vapor.

cards.title: How did basketball begin?
cards.summary: James Naismith invented basketball in Springfield, Massachusetts, in 1891. He was looking for a game people could play indoors in winter.

cards.title: How did people live in ancient Egypt?
cards.summary: In ancient Egypt, much of daily life followed the Nile River. Flooding once left rich mud across nearby fields.

cards.title: How did Roman aqueducts carry water?
cards.summary: A Roman aqueduct carried water from a source, such as a spring, toward a place people needed it. Builders gave the water channel a gentle downhill slope so gravity kept the water moving.

cards.title: How did the modern Olympic Games begin?
cards.summary: The first modern Olympic Games opened in Athens, Greece, in 1896. Organizers drew inspiration from games held long before at Olympia.

cards.title: How did the Nineteenth Amendment change voting?
cards.summary: The Nineteenth Amendment says that a U.S. citizen’s right to vote cannot be denied because of their sex.

cards.title: How did the Rosetta Stone help people read hieroglyphs?
cards.summary: The Rosetta Stone has the same announcement carved in three kinds of writing. One is in Greek, which scholars could already read.

cards.title: How do Egyptian hieroglyphs work?
cards.summary: Ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs are signs used to write the Egyptian language. Some are easy to recognize as pictures, such as an owl or an eye.

cards.title: How do farmers water crops when it does not rain?
cards.summary: Irrigation means bringing water to a place where plants need it. A farm may get water from a river, a well, or a place where water has been stored.

cards.title: How do lungs get oxygen into your body?
cards.summary: When you breathe in, air travels down your windpipe and through branches that get smaller and smaller inside your lungs. At the ends of many branches are clusters of tiny air sacs.

cards.title: How do muscles move your bones?
cards.summary: When you bend your elbow, muscles near your upper arm put a pull on your bones. Strong strips called tendons attach many muscles to bones.

cards.title: How do orchestra musicians play together?
cards.summary: An orchestra is a group of musicians who play different instruments together. A typical orchestra includes strings, woodwinds, brass, and percussion.

cards.title: How do people read braille?
cards.summary: Braille uses patterns of raised dots. A reader feels them with their fingertips.

cards.title: How do written notes tell us what to play?
cards.summary: Written music gives performers a set of marks to follow. In a familiar kind of musical notation, notes sit on or between five lines called a staff.

cards.title: How do you measure area?
cards.summary: Area tells how much flat space a shape covers. Picture a rectangle made of square tiles that all have the same size.

cards.title: How do you score in soccer?
cards.summary: In soccer, two teams try to get the ball into the other team’s goal. A goal counts when the whole ball goes over the goal line between the posts and under the crossbar, as long as the scoring team has not broken a rule.

cards.title: How do your ears hear?
cards.summary: A sound sends vibrations through the air. When those vibrations reach your ear, they make a thin part called the eardrum move.

cards.title: How does a lever make a job easier?
cards.summary: A lever is a stiff piece that turns around a fixed point. A seesaw is a lever, and the support under its middle is the turning point, called a fulcrum.

cards.title: How does a pulley help lift something?
cards.summary: A pulley is a wheel with a groove that guides a rope or cable. Hang one pulley from a support, run a rope over it, and tie a load to one end.

cards.title: How does a woodcut make a picture?
cards.summary: To make a woodcut, an artist carves away the parts of a flat block that should stay blank on the picture. The raised parts that are left get covered with ink.

cards.title: How does American Sign Language work?
cards.summary: American Sign Language, or ASL, is a language that people can see. Signers use their hands, faces, and bodies to express ideas.

cards.title: How does barter work?
cards.summary: Barter means trading something directly for something else. You might trade a comic you have already read for a book a friend has finished.

cards.title: How does your brain send messages?
cards.summary: Reaching for a pencil starts with messages traveling between nerve cells. A nerve cell is called a neuron.

cards.title: How does your heart move blood?
cards.summary: Put a hand over your chest and you may feel your heart beating. Each beat is a squeeze from a muscle about the size of your fist.

cards.title: How erosion carries rock and soil away
cards.summary: Erosion happens when water, wind, ice, or gravity moves soil and bits of rock. Rain can wash dirt from a path into a ditch.

cards.title: How hurricanes get their strength
cards.summary: A hurricane is a large spinning storm that grows over warm ocean water. Warm, moist air rises from the sea.

cards.title: How living things change over generations
cards.summary: Living things often have small differences from others of the same kind. Suppose some beetles have a color that makes it harder for birds to spot them.

cards.title: How magnets pull and push
cards.summary: A magnet can pull some materials toward it without touching them. Iron is one example.

cards.title: How plants make their own food
cards.summary: A green plant uses sunlight, water, and a gas called carbon dioxide to make sugar. This is photosynthesis.

cards.title: How pollen travels from flower to flower
cards.summary: Flowers can make tiny grains called pollen. For many flowers to make seeds, pollen must reach a part of a flower that can receive it.

cards.title: How rainbows form
cards.summary: A rainbow can appear when sunlight shines into water drops in the air. The light bends on its way into a drop, bounces off the inside, and bends again as it leaves.

cards.title: How seeds start new plants
cards.summary: A seed holds the beginnings of a new plant. A coat helps protect the tiny plant inside.

cards.title: How sound moves through the air
cards.summary: Sound starts with something moving back and forth. When you pluck a guitar string, it shakes the air nearby.

cards.title: How the three main kinds of rock form
cards.summary: Scientists group rocks by the way they formed. Igneous rock forms when melted rock cools and hardens.

cards.title: How tiny animals build coral reefs
cards.summary: A coral reef can look like a pile of rocks or plants, but it is built by small animals called coral polyps. Many kinds live in groups.

cards.title: India
cards.summary: India is a country in southern Asia. The Himalayas rise along its north, and a large part of the country reaches south into the Indian Ocean region.

cards.title: Is rhythm the same as the beat?
cards.summary: The beat is the steady pulse you can tap along to in much music. Rhythm is the pattern made by sounds and silences as time goes by.

cards.title: Japan
cards.summary: Japan is a chain of islands off the eastern side of Asia. A group of islands is called an archipelago.

cards.title: Jupiter, the biggest planet
cards.summary: Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and the biggest in our solar system. It is about eleven times as wide as Earth.

cards.title: Kenya
cards.summary: Kenya is in East Africa, and the equator runs across it. Its eastern coast meets the Indian Ocean.

cards.title: Light and the colors we see
cards.summary: Light brings energy from one place to another. The Sun gives off light.

cards.title: Mars, the red planet
cards.summary: Mars looks red from far away because its dust and rocks contain a kind of iron that has rusted. Up close, the ground can also look brown, tan, or gold.

cards.title: Mercury, the closest planet to the Sun
cards.summary: Mercury is the smallest planet in our solar system and the closest one to the Sun. Its rocky ground is covered in round dents called craters.

cards.title: Mexico
cards.summary: Mexico is in North America, just south of the United States. The Pacific Ocean is on one side and the Gulf of Mexico is on the other.

cards.title: Neptune, the farthest planet
cards.summary: Neptune is the eighth planet from the Sun, so a trip around the Sun takes about 165 Earth years. It is cold at the tops of its clouds, and powerful winds sweep across them.

cards.title: Our solar system
cards.summary: The solar system is our Sun and everything held in orbit by its gravity. That includes eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets, and smaller objects such as asteroids and comets.

cards.title: Saturn and its rings
cards.summary: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun. The wide rings around it are made of countless pieces of ice and rock.

cards.title: Solids, liquids, and gases
cards.summary: An ice cube, a puddle, and invisible water vapor are all made of water, but they act differently. In ice, the molecules stay in a pattern and jiggle around their spots.

cards.title: The Sun, our nearest star
cards.summary: The Sun is a star close enough to warm our planet and light up the daytime sky. Other stars can look like tiny dots because they are so far away.

cards.title: The water cycle
cards.summary: The same water can be in the ocean one day and in a cloud another day. Some water at the ocean’s surface changes into a gas and mixes with the air.

cards.title: Tyrannosaurus rex
cards.summary: Tyrannosaurus rex was a large dinosaur that walked on two back legs. Some adults reached about 40 feet long.

cards.title: United States
cards.summary: The United States of America lies in North America and includes 50 states. Most form one connected group between Canada and Mexico.

cards.title: Uranus, the planet on its side
cards.summary: Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun. If Earth’s spin looks a bit like a tilted spinning top, the spin of Uranus looks more like that of a rolling wheel.

cards.title: Venus, the hottest planet
cards.summary: Venus is the second planet from the Sun, almost the same size as Earth. Its air is mostly a gas called carbon dioxide.

cards.title: Weather and climate are different
cards.summary: Weather is what the air outside is like now or over a short stretch of time. It might be windy this morning and sunny this afternoon.

cards.title: What a tornado is
cards.summary: A tornado is a fast-spinning column of air that reaches from a storm to the ground. Tornadoes sometimes grow from large thunderstorms that are already turning.

cards.title: What are the continents?
cards.summary: Continents are Earth’s biggest regions of land. A common way to name them uses seven: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America.

cards.title: What are the three branches of the U.S. government?
cards.summary: The United States divides federal government work among three branches. The legislative branch, Congress, makes federal laws.

cards.title: What are volleyball players trying to do?
cards.summary: Volleyball teams send a ball over a net and try to land it in the other team’s court. They can also score when the other team makes a mistake, such as hitting the ball out.

cards.title: What can a portrait tell us?
cards.summary: A portrait is an artwork about a person or group of people. It could be a painting, a photograph, a drawing, or a sculpture.

cards.title: What did the Declaration of Independence say?
cards.summary: In 1776, the Continental Congress approved a document saying that 13 British colonies in North America were separating from Great Britain. The Declaration of Independence explained why they were taking that step and described rights they said people should have.

cards.title: What do your kidneys do?
cards.summary: Your kidneys help keep the right mix of water, salts, and other materials in your blood. Inside each kidney, tiny filters take some water and small materials out of blood.

cards.title: What does a fraction tell you?
cards.summary: A fraction can tell you how much of a whole you have. Cut a sandwich into four equal parts.

cards.title: What does federalism mean in the United States?
cards.summary: Federalism means that governing power is divided between the national government and the states. The U.S.

cards.title: What does the U.S. National Archives keep?
cards.summary: The U.S. National Archives takes care of records made by the national government that have lasting value.

cards.title: What energy can do
cards.summary: Energy lets things move or change. A rolling ball has energy because it is moving.

cards.title: What fossils tell us
cards.summary: A fossil is something from long-ago life that lasts into the present. It might be part of a shell or a tooth, or a mark left by a leaf or a walking animal.

cards.title: What goes on behind the scenes in a museum?
cards.summary: A museum collects and cares for objects that can teach people something. A museum might hold paintings, historic clothing, fossils, or dried plants.

cards.title: What happened at the ancient Olympic Games?
cards.summary: The ancient Olympic Games were held at Olympia in Greece as part of a festival honoring the god Zeus. Athletes competed in events such as running, wrestling, and chariot racing.

cards.title: What happened to most dinosaurs
cards.summary: About 66 million years ago, most kinds of dinosaurs disappeared. Scientists have strong evidence that a huge asteroid hit Earth at about that time.

cards.title: What is a euro?
cards.summary: The euro is a kind of money used in many European countries, including France. A euro is divided into 100 cents.

cards.title: What is an algorithm?
cards.summary: An algorithm is a set of steps for solving a problem or doing a job. Imagine looking for your name in a list that is sorted from A to Z.

cards.title: What is an alphabet?
cards.summary: An alphabet is a set of letters used to write a language. In an alphabet, letters or groups of letters stand for sounds.

cards.title: What is latitude?
cards.summary: Latitude tells you how far north or south a place is from Earth’s equator. Imagine putting a belt around the middle of a globe.

cards.title: What is longitude?
cards.summary: Longitude tells you how far east or west a place is from the line chosen as zero longitude. This starting line is called the prime meridian.

cards.title: What is phishing?
cards.summary: Phishing is a trick where someone makes a message look trustworthy to get you to give them something or do something. They might ask for a password, send a link that leads to a fake sign-in page, or try to get you to open a file.

cards.title: What is the Library of Congress?
cards.summary: The Library of Congress is a research library in Washington, D.C. It helps people in Congress find information they need and also makes materials available to the public.

cards.title: What is the U.S. Bill of Rights?
cards.summary: The Bill of Rights is the name for the first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution.

cards.title: What is the U.S. Congress?
cards.summary: Congress is the part of the United States government that makes federal laws. It has two parts, called the House of Representatives and the Senate.

cards.title: What is the U.S. Constitution?
cards.summary: The U.S. Constitution sets the basic rules for the United States government.

cards.title: What makes an ecosystem
cards.summary: An ecosystem includes living things in a place, the parts of the place that are not alive, and the ways they affect one another. Think of a pond.

cards.title: What makes lightning and thunder
cards.summary: Inside a storm cloud, bits of ice can bump into each other and help separate electric charges. As the charges build up, electricity can suddenly move through the air.

cards.title: What makes ocean currents flow
cards.summary: An ocean current is water moving from one place to another. In shallow areas near the coast, the tide can make water flow into a bay and later flow out.

cards.title: What makes something a chemical element
cards.summary: A chemical element is a kind of substance made of atoms that all have the same number of protons. Every gold atom has 79 protons, so a very pure piece of gold has atoms of just one element.

cards.title: What minerals are
cards.summary: A mineral is a solid that forms in nature and has a certain kind of material and pattern inside it. Quartz is one mineral.

cards.title: What was ancient Greece?
cards.summary: Ancient Greece included many communities around the sea. Some cities and the area around each city formed a separate government.

cards.title: Where did corn come from?
cards.summary: Corn, also called maize, grew into a farm crop from a wild plant called teosinte. This change began thousands of years ago in what is now Mexico.

cards.title: Where does food go after you swallow it?
cards.summary: Digestion begins before you swallow. Your teeth break up food, and saliva starts breaking down some of it.

cards.title: Where is the equator?
cards.summary: The equator is an imaginary circle around Earth halfway between the North Pole and the South Pole. It divides Earth into the Northern Hemisphere and Southern Hemisphere.

cards.title: Why birds are living dinosaurs
cards.summary: Birds belong to one branch of the dinosaur family. Their early relatives were small, two-legged dinosaurs that lived long before people.

cards.title: Why comets grow tails
cards.summary: A comet is a small body of ice, dust, and rock that travels around the Sun. When a comet comes into warmer parts of the solar system, some of its ice changes straight into gas.

cards.title: Why did ancient Romans build so many roads?
cards.summary: Roads tied ancient Rome to places across its growing territory. A good road made it easier to move travelers, soldiers, animals, and goods over land.

cards.title: Why did people press signs into clay?
cards.summary: In ancient Mesopotamia, people used clay tablets as writing surfaces. A writer used a tool called a stylus to press small wedge shapes into soft clay.

cards.title: Why do computers use 0s and 1s?
cards.summary: A computer can store a tiny piece of information in one of two states. We give those states the names 0 and 1.

cards.title: Why do farmers change crops in a field?
cards.summary: Crop rotation means planning to grow different crops in the same place at different times. If a disease can easily spread among one kind of plant, growing an unrelated plant in that field for a while can leave the disease with fewer plants to infect.

cards.title: Why do flat maps stretch Earth?
cards.summary: The surface of Earth curves, but paper is flat. Any way of drawing that curved surface on a flat page changes something about the places on it.

cards.title: Why do people save seeds in seed banks?
cards.summary: A seed bank stores seeds so people can grow their plants again in the future. It may hold many varieties of one crop.

cards.title: Why do people use money?
cards.summary: Money makes it easier to buy and sell things. Imagine you make a hat and want a book.

cards.title: Why do you need a password?
cards.summary: A password is a secret you enter to help show you are allowed to sign in to an account. If someone else learns it, they may be able to sign in as you.

cards.title: Why does the United States take a census?
cards.summary: A census counts the people who live in a place. The United States takes a census of the whole country once every ten years.

cards.title: Why Earth has seasons
cards.summary: Earth has seasons because the line it spins around is tilted. During part of the year, the northern half leans toward the Sun.

cards.title: Why Pluto is a dwarf planet
cards.summary: Pluto is a small world of rock and ice that goes around the Sun. It is round like a planet, but its gravity does not control its path’s neighborhood.

cards.title: Why the ground shakes in an earthquake
cards.summary: An earthquake can start when rocks on each side of a break in Earth’s crust get stuck. The break is called a fault.

cards.title: Why the Moon changes shape in the sky
cards.summary: The Moon is always round, even when it looks like a thin slice. Usually, sunlight lights up one half of the Moon.

cards.title: Why the ocean has tides
cards.summary: If you leave a stick on the beach, later waves might reach it even though the wind has not changed. The water level rises and falls as part of the tide.

cards.title: Why there are waves in the ocean
cards.summary: Many ocean waves begin when wind pushes on the water’s surface. The pushes add energy.

cards.title: Why volcanoes erupt
cards.summary: A volcano has an opening where hot melted rock can reach Earth’s surface. The melted rock is called magma while it is below ground and lava once it comes out.

cards.title: Why was the Great Pyramid built?
cards.summary: The Great Pyramid at Giza was built as a tomb for Khufu, a ruler of ancient Egypt. It rises from a broad, square base and has four sides that slope toward the top.

cards.title: Why was Yellowstone made a national park?
cards.summary: Yellowstone became a national park in 1872. An important reason was that people wanted to keep its geysers, hot springs, and other unusual natural features protected and open to visitors.
